run.question: My AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 has high latency issues. Investigate why.

report.summary: The question is about AWS Lambda 'payment-processor' in us-east-1, and no data source in this Run can observe Lambda behaviour. Only Jaeger, Prometheus and Kubernetes were queryable; every Prometheus and Jaeger call in this Run returned status error with reason SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no Lambda duration, cold-start, concurrency or log signal was obtained, and the AWS/CloudWatch integration the runbook needs is not among the available data sources. The Kubernetes cluster does not contain the named function at all: the deployment list shows only the OpenTelemetry demo services, and the only payment-related workload is a long-running Kubernetes Deployment 'payment' in namespace otel-demo (pod payment-6f7bc865d6-9z92d, 1/1 ready, started 2026-11-20T16:32:07Z, restart count 2) — a different entity from an AWS Lambda function and not evidence about it. I ran the runbook lambda-performance-troubleshooting and could not carry out any of its five steps for the same reason: step 1 (CloudWatch Duration statistics) — no CloudWatch/AWS metrics source configured, and the only registered metrics source (Prometheus) returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE; step 2 (CloudWatch Logs [ERROR]/[WARN]/timeout filter) — no CloudWatch Logs source; only Kubernetes pod logs are available, which cover the otel-demo 'payment' pod, not the Lambda; step 3 (InitDuration / cold starts) — no CloudWatch; step 4 (ConcurrentExecutions) — no CloudWatch; step 5 (Logs Insights memory-utilization query) — no CloudWatch Logs. No cause for high Lambda latency can be named from this evidence; the assessment is inconclusive, with the missing observability of the Lambda as the gap.

claims.text: The cluster-wide deployment list returned 24 deployments, all in kube-system, local-path-storage or otel-demo (e.g. coredns, metrics-server, ad, cart, checkout, payment, prometheus); no Deployment named 'payment-processor' exists in it.

The otel-demo pod list contains 22 pods, none named 'payment-processor'; the payment-related pod is payment-6f7bc865d6-9z92d, phase Running, restart count 2, started 2026-11-20T16:32:07Z on node opspilot-m1-control-plane, owned by ReplicaSet payment-6f7bc865d6.
The only payment-named Service in namespace otel-demo is 'payment' (TCP port 8080, targetPort 8080); no service or workload named 'payment-processor' appears among the 26 otel-demo services.

Grouping all in-window events by involved object kind/namespace/reason shows otel-demo Pod Unhealthy events (count 5) and a BackOff event (count 1); the detailed otel-demo Unhealthy/BackOff/Killing events name only kube-state-metrics-7cbf5b996-df4sz (liveness/readiness connection refused, container killed 2026-11-22T08:04:50Z), otel-collector-789c64b9bf-tl55c (readiness refused on :13133, 2026-11-22T08:04:22Z) and prometheus-readonly-proxy-f4866f767-62bgn (readiness/liveness refused, nginx BackOff, 2026-11-22T08:04:23Z-08:05:10Z); no event names the payment pod.

The previous nginx container of prometheus-readonly-proxy-f4866f767-62bgn logged at 2026-11-22T08:04:42Z: 'host not found in upstream "prometheus:9090" in /etc/nginx/nginx.conf:22' and exited with the emerg-level nginx failure.

The only line in the local otel-demo 'payment' container logs (2026-11-22T07:53:20Z-08:53:20Z window) matching error/latency terms is '(node:24) MetadataLookupWarning: received unexpected error = Invalid response from metadata service: incorrect Metadata-Flavor header. code = UNKNOWN' at 2026-11-22T08:04:24Z; this is the Kubernetes payment service pod, not the Lambda function, and the line does not mention latency, timeouts or request failures.

The observability path that serves Prometheus to this Run (nginx in prometheus-readonly-proxy) restarted around 2026-11-22T08:04:42Z because it could not resolve upstream 'prometheus:9090'; this may explain why later Prometheus queries returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, but no evidence ties that restart to the 08:53 query failures, so it is only a possible explanation for the missing metrics, not for Lambda latency.

The Kubernetes workload 'payment' in otel-demo is not the subject 'payment-processor' Lambda: it is a long-running Deployment-backed pod (started 2026-11-20T16:32:07Z, before the window) with no payment-specific error or Unhealthy event, so its state neither explains nor evidences the reported Lambda latency.

Configure an AWS CloudWatch (and CloudWatch Logs) data source for us-east-1, then run the lambda-performance-troubleshooting steps against function 'payment-processor': Duration average/maximum per 300s, [ERROR]/[WARN]/timeout log filter, InitDuration cold-start statistics, ConcurrentExecutions maximum per 60s versus the account/function concurrency limit, and the REPORT-based maxMemoryUsed versus memorySize query, comparing a pre-incident baseline window with the incident window.

gaps: No AWS/CloudWatch data source is available in this Run's data sources (only jaeger, prometheus, kubernetes and knowledge are listed), so Lambda Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, memory utilization and Lambda logs for 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 could not be queried at all.

Every Prometheus call in this Run (get_metric_names for traces_/rpc_/http_/app_ and for lambda/aws patterns, execute_prometheus_instant_query count(up), metrics_range_query of payment span rate) returned status error with reason SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no metric series — including any ERROR series — was observed; missing series are unknown, not zero.
Every Jaeger call (traces_list_services, traces_search for service 'payment') returned status error with reason SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no span-level latency or error attribution was possible.

No Kubernetes object, ConfigMap (20 configmaps listed, e.g. flagd-config, otel-collector, prometheus) or event in the cluster references 'payment-processor' or a Lambda function; the exact entity named in the question was not found under that name, and only the unrelated otel-demo Kubernetes 'payment' Service/Deployment exists as a similarly named entity.
Change history is not integrated, so function code, memory-size, timeout, provisioned-concurrency or deployment changes that could explain Lambda latency cannot be inspected.

The authorized window's telemetry (2026-11-21T08:53:20Z-2026-11-22T08:53:20Z) contains no Lambda-side signal, so no statement about when the latency began or whether it deviates from a baseline can be made.
next_steps: Add read-only CloudWatch (metrics and logs) access for us-east-1 and re-check function 'payment-processor' Duration average and maximum at 300s resolution against a pre-incident baseline window.
Query CloudWatch InitDuration count/average to test the cold-start hypothesis and ConcurrentExecutions maximum per 60s against the function's reserved/account concurrency.
Run the CloudWatch Logs Insights REPORT query for max(@maxMemoryUsed) versus avg(@memorySize) to test memory pressure, and filter logs for '[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout' during the latency window.

Inspect the Lambda's downstream dependencies (any external APIs, databases or SDK calls) and its recent version/configuration changes, since latency inside the function may originate in a dependency rather than in the function itself.
Check whether the observability path (prometheus-readonly-proxy nginx failing to resolve 'prometheus:9090' at 2026-11-22T08:04:42Z) keeps the Prometheus/Jaeger sources unavailable for future runs.

If the subject was intended to be the Kubernetes 'payment' service in otel-demo rather than an AWS Lambda, confirm that explicitly, since it is a different entity and its telemetry also could not be read in this Run.

content.name: lambda-performance-troubleshooting
content.content:
# AWS Lambda High Latency Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose and resolve AWS Lambda function performance issues including high latency, timeouts, and cold starts.

## Steps

### Step 1: Query Performance Metrics
Use CloudWatch to check Lambda function latency over time:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name Duration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 2: Check Function Logs
Look for errors or slow operations in CloudWatch Logs:
```bash
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --filter-pattern "[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout" --limit 100
```

### Step 3: Analyze Cold Start Patterns
Query CloudWatch for cold start frequency:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name InitDuration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Count --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 4: Check Concurrent Executions
Verify Lambda isn't hitting concurrency limits:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name ConcurrentExecutions --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 60
```

### Step 5: Review Memory Utilization
Check if function needs more memory allocation:
```bash
aws logs insights start-query --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --start-time <epoch-start> --end-time <epoch-end> \
  --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@maxMemoryUsed), avg(@memorySize)"
```
